cards.front: In cell signalling, what is a receptor?
cards.back: The protein that binds a signalling molecule (the ligand) and passes the news on.
cards.quote: The difference is the receptor, the protein that binds a signalling molecule (the ligand) and passes the news on.

cards.front: Receptor signalling rule: "wiring sets what; steps set when." What does each half mean?
cards.back: What the receptor is wired to (pore, G protein, kinase, gene) picks the effector and so what the signal does. The waits at the steps between binding and output, above all the slowest, set when it starts.
cards.why: Steps that keep running after the ligand leaves set how long the response lasts.
cards.quote: How long the steps between binding and that output take, above all the slowest, sets when it starts

cards.front: Why must most neurotransmitters, peptide hormones and growth factors act on a receptor at the cell surface?
cards.back: They are water-soluble, so the lipid bilayer of the plasma membrane keeps them outside. The receptor must change events inside without letting the ligand through.
cards.quote: Most ligands, such as neurotransmitters, peptide hormones and growth factors, are water-soluble, so the double sheet of fat that is the plasma membrane keeps them outside.
cards.section: The membrane problem: three ways across, and one way around

cards.front: Name the three main ways a receptor passes information across the membrane, and the one way around the problem.
cards.back: Across: open a pore (ligand-gated channel); switch on a G protein (seven-pass receptor); bring single-pass chains together. Around: a fat-soluble ligand such as a steroid enters and meets a receptor inside.
cards.quote: There are three main ways, plus one family whose ligand comes inside: four architectures.
cards.section: The membrane problem: three ways across, and one way around

cards.front: How does a ligand-bound seven-pass receptor switch on a G protein?
cards.back: Binding rearranges the helix bundle so the receptor acts as an exchange factor: it pries GDP out of the G protein, and the empty site fills with GTP because the cell holds far more GTP than GDP.
cards.quote: it pries GDP out of a G protein, and because the cell holds far more GTP than GDP, the empty site fills with GTP.
cards.section: The membrane problem: three ways across, and one way around

cards.front: A G protein is a switch protein, off while it holds {{c1::GDP}} and on while it holds GTP.
cards.quote: A G protein is a switch protein, off while it holds GDP and on while it holds GTP.
cards.section: The membrane problem: three ways across, and one way around

cards.front: Why are receptors for steroid hormones such as estradiol found inside the cell rather than at the surface?
cards.back: Steroids dissolve in fat and slip through the membrane, so they can reach a receptor waiting inside.
cards.quote: Steroid hormones such as estradiol dissolve in fat and slip through the membrane, so their receptors wait inside the cell.
cards.section: The membrane problem: three ways across, and one way around

cards.front: The muscle (nicotinic) acetylcholine receptor is {{c1::five subunits}} arranged around a central pore.
cards.quote: The muscle acetylcholine receptor, the nicotinic type, is five subunits arranged around a central pore.

cards.front: What is a second messenger? Give an example.
cards.back: A small molecule, made by an effector enzyme, that carries the signal on inside the cell. Example: cAMP.
cards.quote: an enzyme that makes a second messenger, a small molecule such as cAMP that carries the signal on inside the cell.

cards.front: Which amino acids do receptor tyrosine kinases phosphorylate, and which do TGF-beta receptors phosphorylate?
cards.back: Receptor tyrosine kinases: tyrosine. TGF-beta receptors (receptor serine/threonine kinases): serine and threonine, with one receptor type phosphorylating the other.
cards.quote: Receptor serine/threonine kinases, such as the TGF-beta receptors, add phosphate to serine and threonine instead, and one receptor type phosphorylates the other.

cards.front: A cytokine receptor chain is mutated so it can no longer hold its JAK kinase. Ligand still binds. Predict the effect on signalling, and why.
cards.back: Signalling fails. Cytokine receptors have no kinase of their own; the ligand works by bringing two chain-bound JAK kinases together, and without JAK there is no kinase to bring together.
cards.quote: Cytokine receptors have no kinase of their own: a JAK kinase stays bound to the inner part of each chain, and the ligand brings two of these kinases together.

cards.front: For single-pass kinase-linked receptors, what is the core move that carries the signal across the membrane?
cards.back: The ligand brings kinase domains together, or rearranges a pair that already exists, so one kinase switches on the other or each switches on its partner.
cards.quote: the ligand brings kinase domains together, or rearranges a pair that already exists, and one switches on the other or each switches on its partner

cards.front: Why does a nuclear receptor such as the estrogen receptor need no second messenger or kinase cascade?
cards.back: The protein that receives the signal acts directly on the gene that answers: once hormone is bound, it holds its DNA sites and recruits coactivators.
cards.quote: There is no second messenger and no kinase cascade, because the protein that received the signal acts directly on the gene that answers.

cards.front: What are the two working parts of a typical nuclear receptor?
cards.back: A pocket that closes around the hormone, and a region that grips a specific stretch of DNA, on one chain.
cards.quote: A typical nuclear receptor is one chain with two working parts: a pocket that closes around the hormone and a region that grips a specific stretch of DNA.

cards.front: An ionotropic receptor is itself an ion channel; a {{c1::metabotropic}} receptor acts through a G protein and other steps inside the cell.
cards.back: Acetylcholine and glutamate each use both kinds.
cards.quote: An ionotropic receptor is itself an ion channel; a metabotropic receptor acts through a G protein and other steps inside the cell.

cards.front: In heart cells, how does acetylcholine bound to the M2 muscarinic receptor open a potassium channel?
cards.back: M2, a GPCR, switches on a G protein; the activated G protein rearranges or dissociates, making its βγ pair available to bind and open the GIRK potassium channel.
cards.quote: The activated G protein rearranges or dissociates, making its βγ pair available to bind a potassium channel called GIRK (G-protein-gated, inwardly rectifying K⁺ channel) and open it.

cards.front: What is a channel's reversal potential, and which way does an open channel move the membrane voltage?
cards.back: The voltage at which the net current through the channel is zero. An open channel pulls the membrane voltage toward it.
cards.quote: An open channel pulls the membrane voltage toward its reversal potential, the voltage at which the net current through it is zero.

cards.front: A skeletal muscle fibre rests near −90 mV. Acetylcholine opens nicotinic channels, which pass sodium and potassium about equally and reverse near 0 mV. Predict the direction of net current and the effect on the fibre.
cards.back: Net inward current, carried mostly by sodium; the fibre depolarizes toward a reversal potential well above threshold, so it is excited.
cards.quote: From −90 mV the net current is inward, carried mostly by sodium, and the fibre depolarizes toward a reversal potential well above threshold.

cards.front: Between beats, a cardiac pacemaker cell climbs from about −60 mV toward a threshold near −40 mV; the potassium equilibrium potential is close to −90 mV. Acetylcholine opens GIRK channels. Predict the effect on heart rate, and why.
cards.back: The heart slows. Potassium flows out (outward current), pulling the membrane down toward −90 mV, so the cell takes longer to reach threshold and the next beat comes later.
cards.why: The G protein here (Gi) also lowers cAMP, which adds to the slowing.
cards.quote: Potassium flows out, the membrane is pulled down, and the cell takes longer to climb to threshold, so the next beat comes later.

cards.front: What general rule decides whether opening a receptor's channel excites or inhibits a cell?
cards.back: Read the effector's ions against their gradients in that cell: a current that reverses above threshold excites; one that reverses below the cell's voltage inhibits.
cards.quote: a current that reverses above threshold excites, and one that reverses below the cell's voltage inhibits.

cards.front: An immature neuron rests at −65 mV and fires at −50 mV. Because it holds extra chloride inside, its chloride equilibrium potential is −45 mV. GABA opens a chloride channel. Predict the effect, and why.
cards.back: It depolarizes and can excite the cell. The open channel pulls the voltage toward −45 mV, which is above the −50 mV threshold.
cards.why: In most adult neurons the chloride reversal lies below rest, so the same channel inhibits.
cards.quote: A GABA-gated chloride channel inhibits most adult neurons but depolarizes immature ones, which hold more chloride inside.

cards.front: A brief pulse of acetylcholine reaches a muscle end-plate and a heart atrial cell. Which current starts sooner, and which outlasts the pulse?
cards.back: The nicotinic end-plate current starts well under a millisecond and decays in about a millisecond. The muscarinic atrial current starts after tens of milliseconds, rises over hundreds, and decays over seconds.
cards.why: The atrial route has a G protein's relay steps between binding and channel; timing alone suggests a G protein but does not prove one.
cards.quote: Timing alone suggests a G protein in the heart, but it does not prove one.

cards.front: A non-hydrolysable GTP analogue is put inside a muscle fibre and an atrial cell. Acetylcholine is applied and then washed away. What happens to each current, and what does it show?
cards.back: The atrial current persists for minutes; the end-plate current is unchanged. G proteins switched on with the analogue cannot switch off, so the atrial route runs through a G protein and the nicotinic pore does not.
cards.quote: The atrial current persists for minutes after the acetylcholine is gone: G proteins switched on with the analogue cannot switch off.

cards.front: Time to the output ≈ {{c1::the sum of the waits at every step}}, from binding to effector.
cards.back: Each step must finish before the next can start.
cards.quote: time to the output ≈ the sum of the waits at every step, from binding to effector

cards.front: Why can the muscarinic route to GIRK, which makes no second messenger, still not respond in under a millisecond?
cards.back: It has a nucleotide exchange (GDP out, GTP in) in the middle, and that exchange is the slow step.
cards.quote: yet with a nucleotide exchange in the middle it cannot respond in under a millisecond. The exchange is the slow step.

cards.front: In heart atrial cells an unaided G protein releases GDP about 0.44 times per minute. Suppose an agonist-bound receptor speeds release 1,000-fold. With mean wait = 1/rate, what is the mean wait for one G protein?
cards.back: Rate: 0.44 × 1,000 = 440 per minute ≈ 7.3 per second. Mean wait: 1/7.3 ≈ 0.14 s, about 140 ms (versus 1/0.44 ≈ 2.3 minutes unaided).
cards.quote: New rate: 0.44 × 1,000 = 440 per minute, about 7.3 per second.

cards.front: G proteins switch on at a constant rate k = 7.3 per second, so the fraction on by time t is 1 − e^(−kt). How long until 10% are on, and why does this matter more than the mean wait for current onset?
cards.back: t = −ln(0.9)/k ≈ 0.105/7.3 s ≈ 0.014 s, about 14 ms. Current starts once some G proteins are on, so the first small fraction sets onset; the mean wait sets the pace.
cards.quote: Setting that to 10% gives t = −ln(0.9)/k ≈ 0.105/7.3 s ≈ 0.014 s.

cards.front: If an agonist-bound receptor sped GDP release only 100-fold (from 0.44 per minute), how long would it take for 10% of G proteins to switch on? What does that imply, given the real atrial current starts after tens of milliseconds?
cards.back: k = 44 per minute ≈ 0.73 per second; t = 0.105/0.73 ≈ 0.14 s, about 140 ms. That is too slow, so the real receptor-driven acceleration must be much larger than 100-fold.
cards.why: Rests on time to output ≈ sum of waits, with exchange the slowest step.
cards.quote: At the 100-fold of the MCAT practice item, a tenth of the G proteins take about 140 ms, which is why the real acceleration must be large.

cards.front: The NMDA glutamate receptor is a channel with no relay step, yet its current rises over about 10 ms, far slower than the muscle nicotinic channel. Does this break the rule that steps set timing?
cards.back: No. The NMDA receptor's own gating is slow, and a slow step counts whichever protein it happens in.
cards.quote: The NMDA receptor's own gating is slow, and a slow step counts whichever protein it happens in.

cards.front: A single-pass kinase receptor adds pairing or rearrangement, phosphorylation and recruitment, so its first output takes {{c1::seconds to minutes}}.
cards.quote: A single-pass kinase receptor adds pairing or rearrangement, phosphorylation and recruitment, hence seconds to minutes.

cards.front: A nuclear receptor has no relay steps at all. Why is its response still slow, tens of minutes to hours?
cards.back: Its output is new RNA and then new protein: new RNA appears within minutes, new protein in tens of minutes to hours.
cards.quote: A nuclear receptor skips every relay step, but its output is new RNA and then new protein.

cards.front: What three things do extra steps in a receptor route buy, at the cost of time?
cards.back: Gain (amplification), a control point at every middle step, and duration.
cards.quote: The extra time buys three things.

cards.front: A ligand-gated channel can pass thousands of ions per opening. Why does it still count as having no catalytic relay, unlike a G-protein route?
cards.back: One receptor opens one pore and makes no enzyme or messenger, although the pore passes many ions. In a G-protein route a catalytic step multiplies: one receptor switches on many G proteins, one adenylyl cyclase makes many messengers. A channel has no middle relay point but can still be tuned at the channel itself.
cards.quote: A directly gated channel has no catalytic relay: one receptor opens one pore, although that pore can pass thousands of ions.

cards.front: What ends a nicotinic response, and what ends a G-protein response?
cards.back: Nicotinic: removal of the transmitter, kept fast by acetylcholinesterase. G protein: hydrolysis of its GTP, which alone takes seconds to tens of seconds, plus destruction of any messengers made.
cards.quote: A G-protein route lasts until the G protein hydrolyses its GTP, which on its own takes seconds to tens of seconds, and any messengers it made are destroyed.

cards.front: A drug inhibits acetylcholinesterase at the muscle end-plate. Predict the effect on the end-plate current, and why.
cards.back: The current lasts longer. The nicotinic response lasts only as long as acetylcholine stays in the cleft, and acetylcholinesterase is what keeps that stay short.
cards.quote: The nicotinic response lasts only as long as the transmitter stays, and acetylcholinesterase keeps that stay short.

cards.front: A drug blocks RGS proteins in atrial cells. Which changes more: how soon the acetylcholine current starts, or how long it lasts after acetylcholine is removed?
cards.back: How long it lasts. RGS proteins speed GTP hydrolysis, the off step, so blocking them keeps G proteins on longer and slows recovery. Onset depends mainly on binding and exchange, so it changes less.
cards.why: In heart cells RGS proteins also speed the rise somewhat, so onset may slow a little.
cards.quote: RGS proteins act on the off step, GTP hydrolysis, so blocking them leaves G proteins on longer and slows recovery.

cards.front: A motor nerve fires up to 50 impulses a second, and each must give one muscle action potential. Could a G-protein route like the atrial one do this job? Why or why not?
cards.back: No. Impulses arrive 1/50 s = 20 ms apart. A G-protein response starts after tens of milliseconds and lasts seconds, so responses would merge. A nicotinic response is over in about a millisecond, before the next impulse.
cards.why: Rests on: onset set by the steps' waits, duration set by the slowest off step.
cards.quote: At 50 impulses a second the impulses are 20 ms apart, so each response is over before the next arrives.

cards.front: A design job: slow the heart's pacemaker within a beat or two, by a tunable amount, recovering over seconds. Choose a receptor route and say what makes it tunable.
cards.back: M2 receptor, G protein, GIRK. Inhibitory, onset tens of ms, offset seconds set by GTP hydrolysis (tuned by RGS proteins). The middle step is the dial: how many G proteins are on sets how much the rate slows.
cards.quote: The middle step is the dial: how many G proteins are on sets how much the rate slows.

cards.front: A design job: commit a stem cell to a new identity that outlasts the signal. Which receptor architecture suits it best, and why is a brief ion current a poor choice?
cards.back: A nuclear receptor (for example the retinoic acid receptor). Hours are fine; it starts a gene program that the new regulatory proteins can keep running after the hormone is gone. A pulse of ions leaves a lasting trace only if it sets off other signals.
cards.why: A single-pass kinase receptor feeding a gene program also works but adds relay steps.
cards.quote: a receptor on the genes starts a program that the new regulatory proteins it makes can keep going after the hormone is gone

cards.front: A transmitter acts in cell A through a GPCR whose G protein opens a potassium channel, and in cell B through a ligand-gated cation channel like the nicotinic receptor. Predict the sign, onset and duration in each cell.
cards.back: A: inhibitory, starts after tens of milliseconds, lasts seconds. B: excitatory, starts well under a millisecond, brief.
cards.why: Wiring (which ions the effector passes) sets the sign; the steps set onset and duration. The molecule does not dictate a single response; the receptor and the cell's wiring supply it.
cards.quote: The molecule does not dictate a single response; the receptor and the cell's downstream wiring supply it.

cards.front: In an ideal unsaturated two-stage enzyme cascade driven by a step input (before depletion or shutoff matters), early output grows as gain × time², so time to a fixed threshold falls as 1/√gain. If gain rises 25-fold, how much sooner is the threshold crossed?
cards.back: √25 = 5, so the threshold is crossed 5 times sooner.
cards.quote: In an ideal unsaturated two-stage enzyme cascade driven by a step input, before depletion or shutoff matters, early output is proportional to gain × time². The time to reach a fixed threshold therefore falls as one over the square root of the gain

cards.front: Adding steps usually delays a response. How can a high-gain GPCR cascade such as rod phototransduction still respond quickly?
cards.back: In an ideal unsaturated two-stage enzyme cascade driven by a step input, early output grows as gain × time², so more gain reaches a fixed threshold sooner (100× gain, 10× sooner). Mammalian rods' dim-flash response peaks within about 100 to 200 ms.
cards.quote: Rod phototransduction is a high-gain GPCR cascade whose dim-flash response in mammalian rods peaks within about 100 to 200 ms.

cards.front: In atrial cells the acetylcholine current is half-maximal near 160 nM. Does that number tell you how fast the response is?
cards.back: No. It is a potency, how much ligand the route needs, which is a separate question from speed.
cards.quote: In atrial cells the acetylcholine current is half-maximal near 160 nM, the number the film quotes; that is a potency, not a speed

cards.front: EGF is a single-chain ligand, unlike dimeric NGF. How does it bring two receptor chains together?
cards.back: It binds one receptor and changes the shape of its ectodomain, exposing a surface that grips a second receptor, so the two kinase domains end up side by side.
cards.quote: A single-chain ligand such as EGF binds one receptor and changes the shape of its ectodomain, exposing a surface that grips a second receptor.
cards.section: How a ligand brings kinase domains together

cards.front: Where does the glucocorticoid receptor wait before its hormone arrives?
cards.back: In the cytoplasm, held by chaperones, until hormone binds.
cards.quote: The glucocorticoid receptor waits in the cytoplasm, held by chaperones, until hormone binds.
cards.section: Other routes across, and nuclear receptors before the hormone

cards.front: How do thyroid hormone and retinoic acid receptors differ from the glucocorticoid receptor before hormone binds, and what does the hormone do?
cards.back: They already sit on DNA without ligand, bound to corepressors; the hormone swaps the corepressors for coactivators.
cards.quote: Thyroid hormone and retinoic acid receptors sit on DNA even without their ligand, bound to corepressors, and the hormone swaps those for coactivators.
cards.section: Other routes across, and nuclear receptors before the hormone

cards.front: How does Notch carry a signal across the membrane without opening a pore, switching on a G protein or pairing kinases?
cards.back: Ligand binding leads enzymes to cut Notch, and the freed inner piece travels to the nucleus, so the receptor becomes its own messenger.
cards.quote: Notch is cut by enzymes when its ligand binds, and the freed inner piece travels to the nucleus itself
cards.section: Other routes across, and nuclear receptors before the hormone
